title: Morgan Stanley breaks down the midterm races it's watching with implications for AI and the data center boom
content:
Wall Street is always on high alert in an election year, but there's a new issue that's motivating voters to get out to the polls this fall: data centers.
Big Tech firms are pouring enormous sums of money into data centers to power their AI ambitions, but the projects are coming up against local opposition that proving effective at stalling or even canceling some projects.
Morgan Stanley in a note last week said that it's watching some big races this November that could have consequences for the data center buildout.
"We've been flagging this as the key wedge issue into the 2026 election since it began to percolate last fall," said strategist Ariana Salvatore. "That being said, we still see this as a state and local policy risk rather than a federal one for the time being."
The investment bank recently highlighted opposition as a potential bottleneck for the AI trade, and a growing number of finance pros are coming to see the data center backlash as a growing risk to the AI trade.
President Donald Trump has even been drawn in, expressing support for data centers in posts on Truth Social. He framed them as a positive economic force that can benefit rural communities. However, as Business Insider's reporting has found, the massive structures can also impose extreme costs on struggling economies and drain key resources.
While Morgan Stanley says that there will likely be more risk for the AI trade following the 2028 presidential election, Salvatore added that her team is monitoring several midterm races closely, as their outcomes could impact planned data center projects. Here are the House and Senate races on their radar.
House:
- Pennsylvania's 8th District: Rob Bresnahan Jr. (R) vs. Paige Cognetti (D) — Bresnahan introduced a bill in June that would make it harder for tech companies to sue communities over zoning issues. What to watch: "Bresnahan's Local Control Protection Act would limit developers' ability to sue municipalities that push back, but it has no cosponsors and has not left committee. Congetti is running on the issue rather than on a mechanism."
- Michigan's 7th District: Tom Barrett (R) vs. William Lawrence (D) — Lawrence has expressed support for a data center moratorium, while Barrett has filed multiple bills aimed at guarding against data center overreach. What to watch: "Lawrence backs a federal moratorium, the vehicle being the Sanders-Ocasio-Cortez AI Data Center Moratorium Act. Barrett introduced the Protecting Local Control of Data Centers Act and the No Data Centers NDAs Act on 20 Aug. All three need federal legislation."
Senate Races:
- Texas: Ken Paxton (R) vs. James Talarico (D) — Rep. Talarico has zeroed in on data center regulation as a key pillar of campaign strategy, including introducing a "Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan." Paxton has been slow to respond to data center related-matters but he recently rolled out a plan to address potentially negative impacts they may pose. What to watch: "Talarico's Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan would end the state sale tax break, set federal minimums and require closed-loop water, but Paxton also backs repealing the exemption, plus rural siting limits and a Chinese technology ban."
- Michigan: Mike Rogers (R) vs. Abdul El-Sayed (D) — Rogers has called for a moratorium on data center construction though he does not support an outright ban. His opponent has been openly critical of data centers, calling for strict regulations and zoning controls. What to watch: "Rogers came out for a one-year Michigan moratorium on 20 Aug while stating he does not support a federal ban. El-Sayed wants comprehensive zoning guidelines, local veto power and community-benefit deals. Neither could impose the Michigan pause."
- Ohio: Jon Husted (R) vs. Sherrod Brown (D) — According to Morgan Stanley, neither candidate has explicitly supported a data center pause, although Brown has described Husted as "the face of data centers" in Ohio. What to watch: "Husted calls siting a local issue. Brown targets tax breaks. Neither explicitly supports a pause."

report.summary: 数据中心成美国中期选举焦点，摩根士丹利警告其影响AI扩张。
report.background: AI热潮推动大型科技公司巨额投资数据中心，但选址引发地方反对，越来越多项目被拖延或取消。数据中心建设因此成为2026年美国中期选举的重要议题。摩根士丹利指出，这类政策风险目前集中在州和地方层面，但联邦层面也可能逐渐介入。特朗普公开支持数据中心，称其利好农村经济，但报道也显示这类设施可能给当地带来资源压力。摩根士丹利追踪多场国会与州长选举，判断结果将影响未来数据中心扩张计划。
key_points: 数据中心遭遇地方反对，成为选举中的‘楔子问题’，可推动或拖累候选人选情，并直接影响科技公司的AI投资计划。
摩根士丹利认为当前风险主要在州和地方层面，联邦层面尚未形成统一政策，但2028年大选后风险可能上升。
在宾州第8选区和密歇根第7选区，候选人提出限制开发商诉讼、支持暂停令等法案，体现地方控制权诉求。
得州和密歇根参议院选举中，双方围绕数据中心税收减免、水耗监管和建设暂停展开辩论，政策分歧明显。
特朗普公开支持数据中心，强调经济效益，但反对者指出其成本与资源消耗，政策博弈将贯穿选举周期。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，数据中心是算力基座，政策不确定性将抬高项目风险和成本，可能推迟AI基础设施投资。开发者可能面临算力资源趋紧或服务涨价，需要更关注项目选址与监管。普通用户将经历AI应用落地速度放缓，但地方社区能获得更多话语权，防止资源被过度消耗。总体而言，这场政治博弈将重新平衡科技扩张与地方权利之间的关系。
report.tools: 可关注 OpenSecrets（选举筹款追踪）、GovTrack（法案进展）、Ballotpedia（候选人与投票信息）；若要跟踪数据中心项目，可关注各州公用事业委员会或当地政府的听证文件，例如 Texas PUC 和 Michigan Public Service Commission。
